intro.title: Counting rows: COUNT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
So far every query showed rows. This quest is about **summarising** them: how many sales, how much money, the average score. The database is new: two weeks of `sales` at a small café chain with three stores, and a class's exam `results`. Open **Tables** to see the columns.

An **aggregate function** turns many rows into one value. `COUNT(*)` counts rows:

```
SELECT COUNT(*) AS sales FROM sales;
```

The result is a single row with a single number. With `WHERE`, only the matching rows are counted:

```
SELECT COUNT(*) AS card_sales FROM sales WHERE payment = 'card';
```

`COUNT(column)` counts only the rows where that column **has a value**, skipping `NULL`. A few payments weren't recorded, so `COUNT(payment)` is smaller than `COUNT(*)`, and the difference is the number of missing values.

```
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_sales, COUNT(payment) AS recorded,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(payment) AS missing
FROM sales;
```

As with any calculated column, name each count with `AS`.

intro.title: SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`SUM(x)` adds up a column, `AVG(x)` gives its average (the mean), and `MIN(x)` and `MAX(x)` the smallest and largest values. Several can go in one query:

```
SELECT SUM(quantity) AS items, MIN(quantity) AS smallest, MAX(quantity) AS largest
FROM sales;
```

They work on calculations too. Each sale's value is `quantity * unit_price`, so the total takings are:

```
SELECT ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue FROM sales;
```

Averages rarely come out round, so they are usually rounded: `ROUND(AVG(score), 1)`.

All of them **skip NULL**. An absent exam doesn't count as 0: `AVG(score)` is the average of the exams that were taken. If you wanted absences to count as 0, you'd divide the sum by every row: `SUM(score) * 1.0 / COUNT(*)`. Which one is right depends on the question.

`MIN` and `MAX` also work on text (alphabetical order) and on dates written as `YYYY-MM-DD`: `MIN(sale_date)` is the first day of sales.

questions.prompt: What does `AVG(score)` give?
questions.explanation: AVG adds the values and divides by how many there are: the mean.

questions.prompt: How do AVG and SUM treat NULL?
questions.explanation: Aggregates ignore NULL values (COUNT(*) is the one that counts every row).

questions.prompt: Which gives the total takings?
questions.explanation: Multiply each row first, then add them up. Multiplying two sums would count every item at every price.

questions.prompt: Which function gives the smallest value?
questions.explanation: MIN gives the smallest value; MAX the largest.

questions.prompt: What does `MIN(sale_date)` give for YYYY-MM-DD dates?
questions.explanation: This date form sorts in date order, so the smallest is the earliest.

questions.prompt: Scores 80, 90 and one absence (NULL). What is AVG(score)?
questions.explanation: The NULL is skipped: (80 + 90) / 2 = 85.

questions.prompt: Same scores. What is `SUM(score) * 1.0 / COUNT(*)`?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all three rows, so the absence counts as 0: 170 / 3.

questions.prompt: Can one query use several aggregates?
questions.explanation: For example `SELECT MIN(x), MAX(x), AVG(x)` gives them all in one row.

questions.explanation: ROUND(AVG(x), 1) keeps it readable.

intro.title: GROUP BY
intro.bodyMarkdown:
One total for the whole table is a start, but questions are usually "per something": sales **per store**, the average **per student**. `GROUP BY` puts the rows into groups that share a value, and the aggregates then work on each group:

```
SELECT store, COUNT(*) AS sales, SUM(quantity) AS items
FROM sales
GROUP BY store;
```

The result has one row per store. Show the grouping column too, or you won't know which number belongs to which group.

**The rule:** every column in `SELECT` must either be in the `GROUP BY` or be inside an aggregate. `SELECT store, product, COUNT(*) … GROUP BY store` makes no sense, because a store has many products. Most databases refuse it; SQLite shows the product from one row of the group, which is an easy-to-miss mistake.

`WHERE` filters rows **before** they are grouped. This counts only the card sales in each store:

```
SELECT store, COUNT(*) AS card_sales FROM sales
WHERE payment = 'card'
GROUP BY store;
```

Rows whose grouping value is `NULL` form a group of their own.

To sort by a total, use its name in `ORDER BY`. The clauses go in this order: `SELECT` … `FROM` … `WHERE` … `GROUP BY` … `ORDER BY` … `LIMIT`.

```
SELECT product, SUM(quantity) AS sold FROM sales
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY sold DESC;
```

intro.title: Grouping by a calculation
intro.bodyMarkdown:
You can group by a calculation as well as by a column. Grouping by the day of the week shows which days are busiest:

```
SELECT strftime('%w', sale_date) AS weekday, COUNT(*) AS sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY weekday;
```

SQLite lets `GROUP BY` use the name you gave the calculation with `AS`, as above. Some databases need the calculation written out again: `GROUP BY strftime('%w', sale_date)`. Both work here.

`CASE` makes your own groups. This splits sales into big and small ones:

```
SELECT CASE WHEN quantity >= 5 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END AS size,
       COUNT(*) AS sales, SUM(quantity) AS items
FROM sales
GROUP BY size;
```

Grouping by a date part gives totals per day, week or month: `strftime('%W', sale_date)` is the week of the year (weeks start on Monday). `COALESCE` can turn the NULL group into a readable one: `GROUP BY COALESCE(payment, 'unknown')`.

With a calculated group, make sure the label says what the group is: `weekday` `3` is a Wednesday.

intro.title: Grouping by several columns
intro.bodyMarkdown:
List several columns after `GROUP BY` and each **combination** becomes a group. Sales per store **and** category:

```
SELECT store, category, COUNT(*) AS sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY store, category;
```

Only the combinations that actually occur appear: if a store sold no tea, there is no `(store, Tea)` row.

As before, every column in `SELECT` must be grouped or aggregated, so a grouped query usually starts with the grouping columns and ends with the totals.

Results with two grouping columns read best when sorted by them, the outer one first. Inside each store, sorting by a total shows the biggest first:

```
SELECT store, category, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY store, category
ORDER BY store, revenue DESC;
```

The order of the columns in `GROUP BY` doesn't change the groups, only the order in `ORDER BY` changes how they're listed.

intro.title: HAVING: filtering groups
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`WHERE` picks **rows** before they are grouped, so it can't use totals: at that point there are none yet. To keep only some **groups**, use `HAVING`, which comes after `GROUP BY` and can use aggregates:

```
SELECT product, SUM(quantity) AS items
FROM sales
GROUP BY product
HAVING SUM(quantity) >= 10;
```

Putting an aggregate in `WHERE` gives the error `misuse of aggregate`. That's the sign it belongs in `HAVING`.

A query can use both. `WHERE` decides which rows go into the groups, and `HAVING` decides which groups are shown. Card sales per store, for the stores with at least 4 of them:

```
SELECT store, COUNT(*) AS card_sales
FROM sales
WHERE payment = 'card'
GROUP BY store
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4;
```

The order of the clauses is now `SELECT` … `FROM` … `WHERE` … `GROUP BY` … `HAVING` … `ORDER BY` … `LIMIT`.

In `HAVING`, write the aggregate out again (`HAVING SUM(quantity) >= 10`). SQLite also accepts the name from `SELECT` (`HAVING items >= 10`), but many databases don't.

A condition that doesn't need a total, such as `store = 'North'`, belongs in `WHERE`: it is clearer and lets the database skip those rows early.

intro.title: COUNT(DISTINCT) and GROUP_CONCAT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts the **different** values instead of the rows. There are 30 sales, but how many different products?

```
SELECT COUNT(*) AS sales, COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS products FROM sales;
```

Per group, it answers questions like "in how many stores was each product sold?":

```
SELECT product, COUNT(DISTINCT store) AS stores
FROM sales
GROUP BY product;
```

Like `COUNT(column)`, it skips `NULL`: `COUNT(DISTINCT payment)` counts the payment methods that were recorded.

`GROUP_CONCAT(column, separator)` joins a group's values into one text, such as a list of the dates a product sold on. `GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT column)` joins each different value once (with `DISTINCT`, SQLite always separates them with a comma).

```
SELECT category, GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT product) AS products
FROM sales
GROUP BY category;
```

The order of the joined values isn't guaranteed. SQLite joins them in the order it reads the rows, which here is the order the sales were added, but don't rely on it for anything important.

In HAVING, `COUNT(DISTINCT …)` finds groups with enough variety: `HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT store) = 3` keeps the products sold in all three stores.

intro.title: Totals with conditions
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`WHERE` and `HAVING` remove rows or groups. Sometimes you want to keep every group but count only some of its rows. Put a `CASE` inside the aggregate:

```
SELECT store,
  COUNT(*) AS sales,
  SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'card' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS card_sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY store;
```

Each card sale adds 1 and every other sale adds 0, so the sum is the number of card sales, next to the total, in the same row.

The same trick adds up only some values: `SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'Coffee' THEN quantity ELSE 0 END)` counts coffees sold. Without the `ELSE`, the other rows give `NULL`, which `SUM`, `AVG` and `COUNT` skip, so `COUNT(CASE WHEN score >= 60 THEN 1 END)` counts the passes and `AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Autumn' THEN score END)` averages the autumn scores only.

Several of these side by side turn rows into columns, a layout often called a **pivot**:

```
SELECT student,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Autumn' THEN score END), 1) AS autumn,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Spring' THEN score END), 1) AS spring
FROM results
GROUP BY student;
```

A percentage is a conditional count divided by all the rows: `ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'card' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1)`.

In SQLite, a comparison is itself 1 (true) or 0 (false), so `SUM(payment = 'card')` also counts card sales. The `CASE` form works in every database.

intro.title: Totals that need care
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A few things about totals catch everyone out at least once.

**The sum of nothing is NULL.** When no rows match, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` give `NULL`, not 0 (only `COUNT` gives 0). Wrap the total in `COALESCE` when 0 is the right answer:

```
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(quantity), 0) AS juice_items FROM sales WHERE category = 'Juice';
```

The same happens inside groups: `SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'Tea' THEN quantity END)` is `NULL` for a store with no tea. `COALESCE(…, 0)` or an `ELSE 0` fixes it.

**Whole-number division.** Sums and counts of whole numbers are whole numbers, so `SUM(score) / COUNT(score)` drops the decimals. Multiply by `1.0` first, or use `AVG`.

**An average of prices is not the price per item.** `AVG(unit_price)` treats a sale of 1 latte like a sale of 10 cookies. The average price actually paid per item is the takings divided by the items: `SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(quantity)`.

```
SELECT ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS average_listed_price,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(quantity), 2) AS paid_per_item
FROM sales;
```

Neither is wrong: they answer different questions. Before writing a total, say in words what it should mean.

intro.title: Summary reports
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A real report often uses every clause at once. It helps to know the order SQL works through them, which is **not** the order they are written in:

`FROM` → `WHERE` → `GROUP BY` → `HAVING` → `SELECT` → `ORDER BY` → `LIMIT`

In words: take the table, keep the rows that match `WHERE`, put them into groups, keep the groups that match `HAVING`, work out the columns (and their `AS` names), sort them, and keep the first few.

That order explains the rules you've met. `WHERE` can't use totals, because grouping comes later. `ORDER BY` can use a name from `SELECT`, because it comes after it. In standard SQL, `WHERE` can't, because it comes before. (SQLite is lenient and accepts it, but most databases give an error, so write the calculation out in `WHERE`.)

A full report, the three best-selling products with more than 20 in takings:

```
SELECT product, SUM(quantity) AS items,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
WHERE payment IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY product
HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 20
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

Read it in the order it runs: from the sales, keep those with a recorded payment, group by product, keep products with more than 20 in takings, work out the columns, sort by takings and keep the first three.

When a report gets long, build it step by step in the sandbox: get the grouping right first, then add the totals, then the filters and the sort.

SELECT store,
  SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%w', sale_date) IN ('0', '6') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS weekend_sales,

challenges.title: Expert: Report cards
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `student` with their autumn and spring averages (`autumn`, `spring`, 1 decimal) and the change from autumn to spring (`change`, 1 decimal). Biggest improvement first.

challenges.solution:
SELECT student,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Autumn' THEN score END), 1) AS autumn,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Spring' THEN score END), 1) AS spring,

challenges.title: Expert: Best days of the week
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the three days of the week with the highest takings: the day's name (`Sunday` to `Saturday`, called `day`), the number of sales (`sales`) and the takings (`revenue`, 2 decimals). Highest first.
challenges.hint: Name the day with a CASE on `strftime('%w', sale_date)` (`WHEN '0' THEN 'Sunday'` …), group by it, then `ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 3`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT CASE strftime('%w', sale_date)
    WHEN '0' THEN 'Sunday' WHEN '1' THEN 'Monday' WHEN '2' THEN 'Tuesday'
    WHEN '3' THEN 'Wednesday' WHEN '4' THEN 'Thursday' WHEN '5' THEN 'Friday'
    ELSE 'Saturday' END AS day,
  COUNT(*) AS sales,
  ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;

It is the other way round

questions.prompt: Which clause runs last?
questions.explanation: LIMIT keeps the first rows after everything else is done.

choices.label: WHERE runs before the rows are grouped

questions.explanation: Each product has one category, so adding it doesn't split the groups, but lets you show it.

questions.prompt: Where do you test "more than 20 in takings"?
questions.explanation: It is a group total.

questions.prompt: Where do you test "payment is recorded"?
questions.explanation: It is about single rows, so filter them early.

intro.title: Easy side quest: Café weekly report
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The café's owner wants a report on the two weeks of `sales`: how each store did, which categories and products sell, how people pay and how the weeks compare.

Takings are always `quantity * unit_price`, rounded to 2 decimals at the end. Each challenge is one table of the report.
intro.sandboxCode:
SELECT store, COUNT(*) AS sales, SUM(quantity) AS items,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY store;

challenges.title: Easy: Store totals
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `store` with its number of sales (`sales`), items (`items`) and takings (`revenue`, 2 decimals). Highest takings first.
challenges.hint: `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(quantity)`, `ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2)`, `GROUP BY store ORDER BY revenue DESC`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT store, COUNT(*) AS sales, SUM(quantity) AS items,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY store
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

challenges.title: Easy: Category totals
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `category` with its items (`items`) and takings (`revenue`, 2 decimals). Highest takings first.
challenges.hint: `GROUP BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT category, SUM(quantity) AS items, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

challenges.title: Medium: Top five products
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the five products with the highest takings: `product`, `items` and `revenue` (2 decimals). Highest first; equal takings in product order.
challenges.hint: `GROUP BY product ORDER BY revenue DESC, product LIMIT 5`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT product, SUM(quantity) AS items, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY revenue DESC, product
LIMIT 5;

challenges.title: Medium: Good days
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `sale_date` on which takings were over 15, with the takings (`revenue`, 2 decimals), in date order.
challenges.hint: `GROUP BY sale_date HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 15 ORDER BY sale_date`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT sale_date, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue FROM sales
GROUP BY sale_date
HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 15
ORDER BY sale_date;

challenges.title: Hard: How people pay
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `store` with its number of sales paid by `card`, `cash` and `app`, and with no payment recorded, in columns called `card`, `cash`, `app` and `unknown`. In store order.
challenges.hint: One `SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'card' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` per method, and `SUM(CASE WHEN payment IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` for unknown.
challenges.solution:
SELECT store,
  SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'card' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS card,
  SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'cash' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cash,
  SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'app' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS app,
  SUM(CASE WHEN payment IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unknown
FROM sales
GROUP BY store
ORDER BY store;

challenges.title: Hard: Week by week
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each week (`strftime('%W', sale_date)`, called `week`) with its number of sales (`sales`), takings (`revenue`, 2 decimals) and average sale value (`average_sale`, 2 decimals). In week order.
challenges.hint: `ROUND(AVG(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS average_sale`, `GROUP BY week ORDER BY week`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT strftime('%W', sale_date) AS week, COUNT(*) AS sales,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS average_sale
FROM sales
GROUP BY week
ORDER BY week;

intro.title: Medium side quest: Exam board
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The exam board is meeting about the class's `results`. They want averages per term, absences, grade counts, the subjects that improved most, and the honour roll.

A missing score means the student was absent. Grades are `A` for 90 or more, `B` for 75 or more, `C` for 60 or more and `D` below that.

challenges.title: Easy: Terms side by side
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `subject` with its autumn and spring averages, rounded to 1 decimal, in columns called `autumn` and `spring`.
challenges.hint: `ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Autumn' THEN score END), 1) AS autumn`, the same for Spring, `GROUP BY subject`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT subject,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Autumn' THEN score END), 1) AS autumn,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Spring' THEN score END), 1) AS spring
FROM results
GROUP BY subject;

challenges.title: Easy: Absences
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `student` and their number of absences (`absent`). Most absences first, then by name.
challenges.hint: `COUNT(*) - COUNT(score) AS absent ... ORDER BY absent DESC, student`.

challenges.title: Medium: Grades per subject
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `subject` with the number of `A`, `B`, `C` and `D` grades, in columns called `a`, `b`, `c` and `d`. Absences don't count.
challenges.hint: `SUM(CASE WHEN score >= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS a`, `SUM(CASE WHEN score >= 75 AND score < 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS b`, and so on. A NULL score fails every condition.
challenges.solution:
SELECT subject,
  SUM(CASE WHEN score >= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS a,
  SUM(CASE WHEN score >= 75 AND score < 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS b,
  SUM(CASE WHEN score >= 60 AND score < 75 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS c,
  SUM(CASE WHEN score < 60 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS d
FROM results
GROUP BY subject;

challenges.title: Medium: Steady students
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `student`s whose lowest score is at least 70, with that score (`lowest`), in name order.
challenges.hint: `MIN(score) AS lowest ... HAVING MIN(score) >= 70 ORDER BY student`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT student, MIN(score) AS lowest FROM results
GROUP BY student
HAVING MIN(score) >= 70
ORDER BY student;

challenges.title: Hard: Most improved subjects
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `subject` and the change from its autumn average to its spring average, rounded to 1 decimal, called `change`. Biggest improvement first.
challenges.hint: `ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Spring' THEN score END) - AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Autumn' THEN score END), 1) AS change ... ORDER BY change DESC`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT subject,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Spring' THEN score END) - AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'Autumn' THEN score END), 1) AS change
FROM results
GROUP BY subject
ORDER BY change DESC;

challenges.title: Hard: Honour roll
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the students who took every exam (no absences) and averaged 80 or more: `student`, `average` (1 decimal) and `taken`. Best average first.
challenges.hint: `HAVING COUNT(score) = COUNT(*) AND AVG(score) >= 80 ORDER BY average DESC`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT student, ROUND(AVG(score), 1) AS average, COUNT(score) AS taken FROM results
GROUP BY student
HAVING COUNT(score) = COUNT(*) AND AVG(score) >= 80
ORDER BY average DESC;

questions.explanation: All rows minus the rows with a score.

questions.prompt: Why does a NULL score not count as a D in `SUM(CASE WHEN score < 60 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`?

choices.label: `NULL < 60` is not true, so it falls to ELSE 0

questions.explanation: Comparisons with NULL are not true.

questions.prompt: Which keeps students with no absences?
questions.explanation: Every row has a score when the two counts are equal.

questions.prompt: Autumn scores are 70 and 78; spring scores are 79 and 80. What does `AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'spring' THEN score END) - AVG(CASE WHEN term = 'autumn' THEN score END)` give?
questions.explanation: A CASE with no ELSE gives NULL for the other term, and AVG skips NULLs, so each AVG sees one term: 79.5 − 74.0 = 5.5.

questions.prompt: Why can't WHERE do the honour roll's "averaged 80 or more"?

choices.label: The average is a group total, so it belongs in HAVING

questions.explanation: WHERE runs before grouping.

questions.prompt: Can HAVING combine two conditions with AND?
questions.explanation: HAVING takes any condition, including several joined with AND.

intro.title: Hard side quest: Product review
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The café is reviewing its menu. For every product, the owner wants to know how it sells, where it sells, how it's paid for, and finally a decision: keep it, watch it or review it.

This side quest uses the whole quest: grouping, `HAVING`, `COUNT(DISTINCT)`, `GROUP_CONCAT`, conditional totals and careful averages.
intro.sandboxCode:
SELECT product, category, SUM(quantity) AS items,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue,
       COUNT(DISTINCT store) AS stores
FROM sales
GROUP BY product, category;

challenges.title: Easy: Product totals
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `product` with its items (`items`) and takings (`revenue`, 2 decimals). Highest takings first, then product.
challenges.hint: `GROUP BY product ORDER BY revenue DESC, product`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT product, SUM(quantity) AS items, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY revenue DESC, product;

challenges.title: Medium: Where it sells
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `product`, the number of different stores selling it (`store_count`) and the list of those stores (`stores`, with `GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT store)`).
challenges.hint: `COUNT(DISTINCT store) AS store_count, GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT store) AS stores`.

challenges.title: Medium: Slow sellers
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the products with fewer than 8 items sold, with their items (`items`). Fewest first, then by product.
challenges.hint: `HAVING SUM(quantity) < 8 ORDER BY items, product`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT product, SUM(quantity) AS items FROM sales
GROUP BY product
HAVING SUM(quantity) < 8
ORDER BY items, product;

challenges.title: Hard: Price paid per category
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `category` with the plain average of its `unit_price` (`listed`) and the price paid per item (`paid`), both rounded to 2 decimals.
challenges.hint: `ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS listed, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(quantity), 2) AS paid`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT category,
  ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS listed,
  ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(quantity), 2) AS paid
FROM sales
GROUP BY category;

challenges.title: Hard: Paid by card
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `category` and the percentage of its sales paid by card, rounded to 1 decimal (`card_percent`). Highest first, then by category.
challenges.hint: `ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'card' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT category,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN payment = 'card' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS card_percent
FROM sales
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY card_percent DESC, category;

challenges.title: Hard: The decision
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each `product` with `items`, `revenue` (2 decimals), `stores` (how many different stores sold it) and a `decision`: `keep` if 10 or more items sold, otherwise `review` if only one store sold it, otherwise `watch`. Highest takings first, then product.
challenges.hint: `CASE WHEN SUM(quantity) >= 10 THEN 'keep' WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT store) = 1 THEN 'review' ELSE 'watch' END AS decision`. Aggregates can go inside CASE.
challenges.solution:
SELECT product, SUM(quantity) AS items,
  ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS revenue,
  COUNT(DISTINCT store) AS stores,
  CASE
    WHEN SUM(quantity) >= 10 THEN 'keep'
    WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT store) = 1 THEN 'review'
    ELSE 'watch'
  END AS decision
FROM sales
GROUP BY product
ORDER BY revenue DESC, product;

questions.prompt: Can an aggregate go inside CASE?
questions.explanation: In a grouped query, CASE can test group totals.

questions.prompt: Which lists the stores that sold a product?
questions.explanation: GROUP_CONCAT joins them into one text; COUNT(DISTINCT) only counts them.

questions.prompt: Why might `listed` and `paid` differ?

choices.label: Big sales of cheap items pull the paid price down

questions.explanation: The price paid per item weights each price by how many were sold.

questions.prompt: Which clause keeps only the slow sellers (fewer than 8 items)?
questions.explanation: It tests a group total.

questions.prompt: A product sold 3 items in North and 4 in South. What does `CASE WHEN SUM(quantity) >= 10 THEN 'keep' WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT store) > 1 THEN 'watch' ELSE 'review' END` give for it?
questions.explanation: 7 items is under 10, so the first WHEN fails. It sold in 2 stores, so the second WHEN is true: `'watch'`.

questions.explanation: Card sales divided by all sales, times 100.0.
